Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-XXXIII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: THESIS I. AD intelligentiam & elucidationem multarum quaestionum, quae circa gratiam & liberum arbitrium, magna contentione animorum, agitantur, plurimum conducit nosse varias acceptiones & distinctiones gratiae, quae usitatae sunt in Scholis Christianis. Itaque non parum facit ad scopum nostrum, qui est lucem aliquam inferre controversiis illis, quae Scholas Christianas exercent & dividunt, si acceptiones & distinctiones istas, quantum fieri poterit, breviter & dilucide exponamus.
english: Thesis I. Many questions about grace and free choice are argued with great heat, and to understand and clear them up it helps a great deal to know the various senses and distinctions of grace used in the Christian schools.
Our aim is to throw some light on the controversies that occupy and divide those schools. So it will serve that aim well if we set out these senses and distinctions as briefly and clearly as we can.

source_text: II. Ut autem a Schola Romana ordiamur, observant ejus Theologi, ut inter alios Bellarminus * & Gulielmus Estius, † gratiae vocabulum generalissime sumptum bifariam accipi. Et primo quidem notare ipsum Dei amorem & benevolentiam, per quam hominibus bene vult & facit: deinde etiam quodcunque gratuitum Dei beneficium, & omne illud quod gratiose nobis a Deo conceditur. Ac duplicem hanc gratiae notionem usitatam esse agnoscunt, tum in scriptura divina, tum apud scriptores Ecclesiasticos, & ipsos etiam Scholasticos Doctores. Priorem illam gratiam, gratiam aeternam & increatam vocant: alteram vero gratiam temporariam & creatam. Et eodem recedit quod alii, cum Estio, dicunt, Gratiam, scilicet, intelligi posse, vel ex parte Dei, vel ex parte nostra. * Lib. 1. de gratia & lib. Arb. c. 1. & 2. † In dist. 26. lib. 2. sententiarum Sect. 1.
english: Thesis II. To begin with the Roman School: its theologians, Bellarmine and William Estius among others, observe that the word 'grace', taken in its most general sense, is used in two ways.

First it means God's own love and goodwill, by which he wishes men well and does them good. Second, it means any free benefit from God, anything he grants us graciously. They acknowledge that both senses are current in Holy Scripture, in the church writers, and in the scholastic doctors themselves.
The first they call eternal and uncreated grace, the second temporal and created grace. What others say with Estius comes to the same thing: grace can be understood either on God's side or on ours.

source_text: III. Porro cum non solum quae naturam superant gratuito nobis a Deo donentur, sed ipsa naturae bona, absque ullis nostris meritis, ex gratuita Dei benignitate habeamus, idcirco gratia latissime sumpta, ut Doctores iidem observant, naturae non opponitur, sed naturam ipsam comprehendit: quae quandoque gratiae nomine designatur, propterea quod est gratuitum quoddam Dei beneficium, gratis nobis a Deo collatum. Verum haec acceptio gratiae est quidem frequens in usu communi, in quo naturae dotes atque commoda gratiae divinae ascribere solemus, sed in scripturis & Scholis rarissima, & parum usitata est. Plerunque enim ibi gratia restringitur ad illa Dei beneficia quae naturae ordinem excedunt, neque ex natura fluunt, aut ad eam constituendam & conservandam necessaria sunt, sed ex gratuita Dei benignitate ipsi superaddita.
english: Thesis III. God gives us freely not only what surpasses nature: the goods of nature themselves we also have from his free kindness, without any merit of ours. So grace in its widest sense, as the same doctors observe, is not set against nature but includes nature itself, which is sometimes called grace because it is a free benefit God has given us for nothing.
This sense is common enough in ordinary speech, where we credit the gifts and advantages of nature to God's grace. In Scripture and in the schools it is very rare and little used.

There grace is usually confined to those benefits of God that go beyond the order of nature: they do not flow from nature and are not needed to make it what it is or to preserve it, but are added to it by God's free kindness.

source_text: IV. Et hoc sensu gratia opponitur naturae. Quoniam illa dona quae nobis supra naturam a Deo conferuntur, singulari quodam modo gratuita sunt: quia, scilicet, non tantum sub meritum personae non cadunt, sed neque naturae debentur. Quamvis enim Deus absolute nihil cuiquam debeat, neque ad quicquam obligetur, tamen ex hypothesi quod creaturam velit esse & operari, illi quodammodo ea praestare debet, sine quibus nec esse, nec operari potest.
english: Thesis IV. In this sense grace is set against nature. The gifts God confers on us above nature are free in a special way: they do not fall under the person's merit, and they are not owed to nature either.

God, absolutely speaking, owes nothing to anyone and is bound to nothing. Yet once he wills that a creature should exist and act, he must in a way supply it with whatever it cannot exist or act without.

source_text: V. Caeterum gratia illa naturae opposita a nonnullis Scholae Romanae Doctoribus sedulo distinguitur in eam quae homini ante lapsum collata est, & eam quae homini lapso per meritum Christi confertur. Ac priorem illam gratiam vocant, gratiam Adami: Posteriorem vero gratiam Christi. Prior ab illis dicitur gratia sanitatis: haec vero posterior gratia Medicinalis. Prior collata est homini non merenti: posterior etiam indigno.
english: Thesis V. Some doctors of the Roman School take care to divide this grace that is set against nature into two: the grace given to man before the fall, and the grace given to fallen man through Christ's merit.

They call the first the grace of Adam and the second the grace of Christ; the first the grace of health and the second healing grace. The first was given to a man who had not earned it, the second to one who was actually unworthy of it.

source_text: VI. Hanc distinctionem, ut maximi momenti, saepius inculcat & urget Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis libro cui fecit titulum Augustinus. Ubi gratiae istius utriusque discrimen, prolixe ex Augustino colligit & explicat. Illud autem discrimen in eo constituit, quod gratia data homini ante lapsum adjutorium erat, sine quo primus homo non poterat velle bonum; sed quod non praestabat ut bonum actu vellet. Gratia vero quam Christus homini lapso largitur, efficit ut homo actu velit, & est auxilium, non simpliciter sine quo, sed quo ipsum velle bonum in homine producitur.
english: Thesis VI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, presses this distinction again and again as of the greatest weight in the book he titled Augustinus, where he collects and explains the difference between the two graces at length from Augustine.
He puts the difference here. The grace given to man before the fall was a help without which the first man could not will good, but it did not make him actually will it.
The grace Christ gives fallen man makes him actually will. It is not merely a help without which, but a help by which the willing of good is itself produced in him.

source_text: VII. Nam observat vir ille adjutoria voluntatis duplicis esse generis. Adjutorium unum esse sine quo voluntas velle non potest, sic tamen ut velle & nolle, uti vel non uti adjutorio, in ejus libero relinquatur arbitrio: aliud quo fit determinate ut voluntas velit. Ac gratiam hominis integri pertendit adjutorium fuisse primi generis, gratiam vero qua Christus hominem corruptum sanat adjutorium secundi generis. In eo, inquit, utriusque gratiae, sanitatis & medicinalis differentia in eo sita est, quod illius primae integritatis adjutorium sic adjuvabat voluntatem, ut cum eo operaretur ipsa, si vellet; nunc autem ipsum adjutorium facit ut velit. Hoc est, adjutorium ante ruinam erat tale, ut influxus adjutorii, perinde atque voluntatis in opus, ab ipso liberae voluntatis nutu penderet, adeoque salva maneret illa libertatis in utramque partem flexibilis indifferentia: nunc vero post ruinam tale est, ut faciat annuere, & influere, & velle voluntatem. De Gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 2. cap. 4.
english: Thesis VII. For he observes that the will's helps are of two kinds. One is a help without which the will cannot will, yet in such a way that willing or not willing, using the help or not using it, is left to its free choice. The other is a help by which it is determinately brought about that the will wills.

He holds that the grace of man in his integrity was a help of the first kind, and that the grace by which Christ heals corrupt man is a help of the second kind. 'The difference between the two graces, of health and of healing,' he says, 'lies in this: the help of that first integrity so helped the will that the will itself might work with it, if it chose; now the help itself makes it will.

That is, before the ruin the help was such that its influence on the work, just like the will's, hung on the free will's own nod, so that the indifference of liberty, able to bend either way, remained intact. Now, after the ruin, it is such that it makes the will assent, and flow into the work, and will' (De gratia Christi salvatoris, book 2, chapter 4).

source_text: VIII. Quibus conformiter toto opere docet praecipuum hoc esse discrimen inter gratiam primi Adae & secundi Adae, quod illa dabat operari bonum, si homo vellet: haec dat insuper ut velit. Illa subjecta fuerat nutui & potestativo dominio voluntatis: haec suo nutui & dominio voluntatem subjicit. Illa pedissequali obsequio ductum voluntatis sequebatur: haec imperioso principatu voluntatem trahit quasi pedissequam. Illa superabiliter & declinabiliter voluntatem praeeuntem comitabatur: haec insuperabiliter & indeclinabiliter voluntatem subsequentem ducit & agit.
english: Thesis VIII. In keeping with this he teaches throughout the work that the chief difference between the grace of the first Adam and that of the second is this: the first gave man the power to do good if he willed, while the second gives him besides the willing itself.

The first was subject to the will's nod and to its power of command; the second subjects the will to its own nod and command. The first followed the will's lead with the obedience of a servant at its heels; the second, ruling with authority, draws the will after it like such a servant.
The first went along with the will as the will went ahead, and could be overcome and turned aside. The second leads and drives the will as it follows, and can be neither overcome nor turned aside.

source_text: IX. Verum quanquam hac in parte Jansenius multos sectatores habeat, eos nempe qui singulari modo se discipulos Augustini vocant, haec tamen illius doctrina rejicitur a maxima Scholae Romanae parte: eique palam repugnant, tam qui Molinae Jesuitae Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, quam qui recentiores Thomistae appellantur. Nam priores illi volunt gratiam Christi, non minus quam gratiam primo homini nondum lapso collatam, sic in potestate voluntatis esse, ut pro innata libertate, illa uti, vel non uti possit, & reipsa saepe non utatur: adeoque a libero arbitrio pendere, ut gratia Christi sit efficax, vel non efficax; & effectum suum in hominis conversione obtineat, vel non obtineat.
english: Thesis IX. On this point Jansenius has many followers, namely those who call themselves disciples of Augustine in a special sense. Even so, this teaching of his is rejected by most of the Roman School. Both the followers of the method and teaching of Molina the Jesuit and those called the recent Thomists openly oppose it.

The first group hold that the grace of Christ, no less than the grace given to the first man before he fell, is in the will's power in such a way that, by its inborn liberty, the will can use it or not use it, and in fact often does not.
So, on their view, it depends on free choice whether Christ's grace is efficacious or not, and whether it achieves its effect in a man's conversion or fails to.

source_text: X. Contra vero qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores, putant gratiam praedeterminantem, & voluntatem ad bonum efficaciter applicantem ab innocentiae statu non fuisse alienam. Et Adam, si quid boni ante peccatum egit, ut egit proculdubio, illud egisse vi cujusdam gratiae Physice voluntatem illius praedeterminantis, eique non tantum boni facultatem largientis, sed illam efficaciter ad bonum praemoventis; sine qua efficaci Dei praemotione, voluntas hominis in nullo ejus statu, juxta ipsorum principia, ad bonum ferri potest.
english: Thesis X. Those called the recent Thomists, on the other hand, think that a grace which predetermines the will and applies it efficaciously to good was not foreign to the state of innocence.

If Adam did any good before he sinned, as he certainly did, he did it, they say, by the power of a grace that physically predetermined his will: a grace that did not merely give his will the ability to do good but efficaciously moved it to good beforehand.
On their principles, without this efficacious premotion from God man's will cannot be carried toward good in any of its states.

source_text: XI. Porro gratia quae per Christum homini corrupto confertur, communiter in Schola Romana distingui solet, in gratiam quam vocant gratis datam, & in gratiam gratum facientem. Quae partitio, ex Doctorum Scholae istius mente, sic accipienda non est, quasi aliqua sit gratia non gratis data; nam quam vocant gratum facientem agnoscunt etiam esse gratuito donatam: Sed quod alibi saepe fit, uni speciei quae proprio nomine caret, relinquunt nomen generis, ut monet Bellarminus loco supra citato.
english: Thesis XI. The grace conferred on corrupt man through Christ is commonly divided in the Roman School into what they call grace freely given and the grace that makes pleasing.
In the minds of that School's doctors the division is not meant to imply that some grace is not freely given, for they grant that the grace that makes pleasing is also given freely.
Rather, as often happens elsewhere, one species that has no name of its own is left with the name of the genus, as Bellarmine points out in the place cited above.

source_text: XII. Igitur gratia gratis data ipsis est donum supernaturale, absque ullo debito, ad aliorum spiritualem salutem praecipue collatum. Gratia vero gratum faciens donum supernaturale, absque ullo debito, ad propriam uniuscujusque salutem spiritualem potissimum datum. Licet enim commune sit gratiae gratis datae cum gratia gratum faciente, ut tam propriae quam alienae saluti conducant: tamen illud interest, quod gratia gratum faciens datur potissimum ad propriam salutem illius qui accipit; secundario vero ad salutem aliorum: nimirum ut nos ipsi primum sancti justique efficiamur, deinde caeteri videant opera nostra bona, & glorificent Patrem nostrum qui in coelis est. Contra vero gratia gratis data alienam salutem spectat praecipue. Constat enim iis donis quae directe & per se, ad salutem ejus in quo sunt, non conducunt; sed multum juvant ad alios ad poenitentiam & fidem adducendos.
english: Thesis XII. So for them grace freely given is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for the spiritual salvation of others. The grace that makes pleasing is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for each person's own spiritual salvation.

Both kinds serve the salvation of the receiver and of others alike. The difference is that the grace that makes pleasing is given chiefly for the salvation of the one who receives it and only secondarily for others: first we ourselves are to be made holy and righteous, and then others are to see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven.

Grace freely given, by contrast, looks chiefly to the salvation of others. It consists of gifts that do not of themselves directly serve the salvation of the person in whom they are, but are a great help in bringing others to repentance and faith.

source_text: XIII. Itaque ad gratiam gratis datam pertinent sermo scientiae, sermo sapientiae, donum prophetiae, discretio spirituum, genera linguarum, operatio virtutum, gratia sanitatum, & plura ejusmodi quae Apostolus enumerat capite duodecimo prioris ad Corinthios, inter quae dona quaedam sunt, ex quibus beneficia corporalia consequuntur, ut bona valetudo, ex gratia sanitatum; sed quia praecipuus atque ultimus finis omnis gratiae gratis datae est salus animae sempiterna, idcirco omnem ejusmodi gratiam, ad aliorum salutem spiritualem conferri in superius allata definitione dictum est.
english: Thesis XIII. Grace freely given therefore includes the word of knowledge, the word of wisdom, the gift of prophecy, the discerning of spirits, kinds of tongues, the working of miracles, the gift of healing, and the other gifts of this kind that the Apostle lists in 1 Corinthians 12.

Some of these gifts bring bodily benefits, as the gift of healing brings good health. But since the chief and final end of all grace freely given is the eternal salvation of the soul, the definition given above said that all such grace is conferred for the spiritual salvation of others.

source_text: XIV. Sub gratia vero gratum faciente comprehendunt ea omnia in quibus aliqua pars, vel initium salutis & justitiae consistit: & quae hominem vel Deo gratum & amicum reddunt, vel ad reconciliationem & amicitiam cum Deo disponunt, & ad hoc per se diriguntur. In quo genere sunt fides, spes, bona voluntas, imo qualecunque fidei, & bonae voluntatis initium, poenitentia, remissio peccatorum, charitas, justitia, bona opera, virtutes earumque augmenta, perseverantia, ac denique vita aeterna, ad quam, tanquam ad gratiam consummatam, priora illa Dei beneficia destinantur. Et de qua dicit Apostolus Rom. 6. Gratia Dei vita aeterna. Ut videre est apud Estium in 2. sentent. dist. 26. paragr. 1.
english: Thesis XIV. Under the grace that makes pleasing they include everything in which any part or beginning of salvation and righteousness consists: everything that either makes a man pleasing to God and his friend, or disposes him to reconciliation and friendship with God and is of itself directed to that end.

To this class belong faith, hope and good will, indeed any beginning at all of faith and good will; repentance, the forgiveness of sins, charity, righteousness, good works, the virtues and their growth, perseverance, and finally eternal life itself. Those earlier benefits of God are destined for eternal life as for grace brought to completion, and of it the Apostle says, 'The grace of God is eternal life' (Romans 6). So Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26, paragraph 1.

source_text: XV. Porro gratiam illam gratum facientem vocant, quia aliquid in homine ponit quod Deo placet, eique probatur, & hominem, quadantenus saltem, & aliquo respectu, Deo gratum & placentem reddit. Neque tamen eorum mens est, gratiam illam quam in homine ponunt, & gratum facientem vocant, omnem divinae dilectionis actum erga nos praevenire, & esse proprie causam amoris quo Deus hominem prosequitur. Nam docent gratiam illam esse simul divini amoris effectum & objectum. Procedit enim ab illo amore, quo Deus homini bene vult: cum sit maximum bonum quod Deus homini conferat: & eatenus est amore divino posterior. Sed simul est aliquid Deo maxime placens, & cujus respectu homo non potest non esse Deo gratus: & eatenus est objectum divini amoris, & divinam erga nos dilectionem aliqua ratione praecedit.
english: Thesis XV. They call it the grace that makes pleasing because it places in a man something that pleases God and wins his approval, and so makes the man, at least to some degree and in some respect, pleasing and acceptable to God.

They do not mean that the grace they place in man under that name comes before every act of God's love toward us, or is strictly the cause of the love God bears him. They teach that this grace is at once the effect and the object of God's love.

It comes from the love by which God wishes man well, being the greatest good God bestows on him, and to that extent it comes after God's love. At the same time it is something highly pleasing to God, and because of it a man cannot fail to be pleasing to him. To that extent it is the object of God's love and in some way comes before his love for us.

source_text: XVI. Caeterum gratiam gratum facientem Schola Romana dividit in gratiam actualem, & gratiam habitualem, seu quod pene eodem recidit, in gratiam permanentem, & gratiam Auxilii specialis, ut mavult loqui Bellarm. lib. 1. de Gratia & libero Arbitrio cap. 2. Et revera discrimen aliquod notari potest inter gratiam actualem, & inter gratiam istam auxilii specialis. Nam per gratiam quae dicitur auxilii specialis, non ipsae bonae actiones nostrae, sed potius eorum quoddam principium significatur: bona vero nostra opera sunt gratia quaedam actualis, & sub ea comprehenduntur.
english: Thesis XVI. The Roman School divides the grace that makes pleasing into actual and habitual grace, or, which comes to nearly the same thing, into permanent grace and the grace of special help, as Bellarmine prefers to put it (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 2).

There is in fact some difference to be noted between actual grace and this grace of special help. The grace of special help means not our good actions themselves but rather a kind of principle of them, whereas our good works are themselves a kind of actual grace and fall under that term.

source_text: XVII. Verum haec divisio, quanquam communiter recepta, a non nemine tamen improbata est. Nam quod sit aliqua Dei Actualis in homine gratia, a nullo quidem inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae unquam dubitatum fuit. At vero secus est de gratia habituali. Agnoscunt enim Doctores Scholastici, in Ecclesia Romana rem non fuisse antehac ita certam, & videri solum definitam esse in Concilio Viennensi sub Clemente V. & in Synodo Tridentina superiori saeculo: prius vero fuisse aliquatenus dubium atq; problematicum, An daretur aliqua gratia habitualis.
english: Thesis XVII. Commonly accepted as this division is, someone has nevertheless rejected it. No theologian of the Roman Church has ever doubted that there is some actual grace of God in man. Habitual grace is another matter.

The scholastic doctors admit that in the Roman Church the point was not formerly so settled. It seems to have been defined only at the Council of Vienne under Clement V and at the Council of Trent in the last century; before that it was somewhat doubtful and open to dispute whether any habitual grace is given.

source_text: XVIII. Et certe Albertus Pighius Doctor non incelebris, paulo ante tempora Concilii Tridentini, ausus est hac in parte communi sententiae Scholae Romanae sese opponere. Haec enim, referente Bellarmino, sunt illius verba libro quinto de Libero Arbitrio. Gratiae acceptionem variam, non ex Scholis, sed ex divinis scripturis petemus. Quandoquidem in illis fere imaginantur qualitatem aliquam increatam animae nostrae a Deo; vel eandem cum charitatis habitu, vel distinctam ab eodem. Quae commentitia universa existimo, nec ex scripturis ullam authoritatem habere.
english: Thesis XVIII. Indeed Albert Pighius, a doctor of some fame, dared on this point to set himself against the common view of the Roman School a little before the time of the Council of Trent.

As Bellarmine reports, these are his words in the fifth book of his work On Free Choice: 'We shall look for the various senses of grace not in the schools but in Holy Scripture. For in the schools they generally imagine some quality created in (increatam) our soul by God, either the same as the habit of charity or distinct from it. I judge all this to be invented, with no authority from Scripture.'

source_text: XIX. Et quanquam hodie nullus est post Concilium Tridentinum, qui Pighium sequatur; & sententia ejus communiter damnetur, saltem ut valde temeraria: nihilominus adhuc inter se disputant Scholae Romanae Theologi An de fide sit dari gratiam habitualem, & an Concilia praedicta intenderint rem illam, tanquam de fide definire. Quod post Concilium Tridentinum, negavit Dominicus Soto Doctor insignis, qui illi interfuit. Licet communiter alii sentiant probabilius esse quod dogma istud sit de fide.
english: Thesis XIX. Since the Council of Trent nobody follows Pighius, and his view is commonly condemned, at the least as very rash. Even so, the theologians of the Roman School still argue among themselves whether it is a matter of faith that habitual grace is given, and whether those councils meant to define the point as of faith.
After the Council of Trent, Domingo de Soto, a distinguished doctor who had been present at it, denied that they did. Others commonly hold it more probable that this teaching is of faith.

source_text: XX. Jam autem sub gratia habituali comprehendunt omnes habitus virtutum infusos, ac praesertim gratiam illam in qua consistere volunt justitiam per quam formaliter coram Deo justificamur: quae ab iis dicitur Gratia justificans, & plerumque Gratia simpliciter & sine addito: & ad quam in communi usu, gratiae gratum facientis nomen restringi solet.
english: Thesis XX. Under habitual grace they include all the infused habits of the virtues, and above all the grace in which, on their view, consists the righteousness by which we are formally justified before God.
They call this justifying grace, and usually just 'grace' with nothing added, and in common usage the name 'grace that makes pleasing' is usually confined to it.

source_text: XXI. Etenim sciendum est apud scriptores Ecclesiae Romanae, gratiam gratum facientem ordinarie sumi sensu longe strictiore, quam sumitur in modo allata divisione. Juxta quam ita opponitur gratiae gratis datae, ut sub se comprehendat omne donum internum, quod per se salutem accipientis juvat, atque ad eam dirigitur. Nam per gratiam gratum facientem intelligunt habitum & qualitatem quandam, per quam homo proprie & formaliter justus constituitur; adeoque simpliciter Deo gratus & amicus. De qua gratia multas inter se versant quaestiones, quarum haec praecipua est, An gratia illa sit habitus aliquis a charitate distinctus, an vero omnino idem cum charitate.
english: Thesis XXI. It should be understood that writers of the Roman Church ordinarily take the grace that makes pleasing in a far narrower sense than in the division just given. There it is set against grace freely given in such a way that it covers every inward gift that of itself helps the receiver's salvation and is directed to it.
In the narrower sense they mean by it a habit, a kind of quality, by which a man is properly and formally made righteous and so simply pleasing to God and his friend.
They debate many questions among themselves about this grace. The chief is whether it is a habit distinct from charity or entirely the same as charity.

source_text: XXII. Et quidem Thomas Scholae Romanae princeps, & alii plurimi docent gratiam illam justificantem & gratum facientem esse qualitatem quandam realiter distinctam a charitate, & reliquis omnibus habitibus virtutum. Quippe volunt gratiae subjectum esse ipsam animae substantiam, in qua immediate sedem suam habeat: charitatis autem, & aliarum virtutum subjectum esse animae potentias, mentem, scilicet, atque voluntatem. Existimant enim ita se habere gratiam ad virtutes infusas, quemadmodum se habet anima ad suas potentias. Et sicut anima dat esse naturale corpori; ex ipsa autem potentiae fluunt, quae sunt animae instrumenta: sic etiam gratiam, de qua jam quaestio est, dare animae esse quoddam supernaturale: ex ipsa vero quodammodo fluere habitus virtutum infusarum, quae sunt principia proxima operationis supernaturalis.
english: Thesis XXII. Thomas, the prince of the Roman School, and very many others teach that this justifying grace that makes pleasing is a quality really distinct from charity and from all the other habits of the virtues.

They hold that the subject of grace is the very substance of the soul, where it has its seat directly, while the subject of charity and the other virtues is the soul's powers, that is, the mind and the will. In their view grace stands to the infused virtues as the soul stands to its powers.

The soul gives natural being to the body, and from it flow the powers that are its instruments. In the same way the grace in question gives the soul a kind of supernatural being, and from it flow, in a manner, the habits of the infused virtues, which are the proximate principles of supernatural action.

source_text: XXIII. Nonnulli contra, ut Durandus, nihil omnino interesse volunt inter gratiam, & charitatem: ac nequidem ratione, sed solo nomine distingui affirmant. Neque magis distinctas esse charitatem & gratiam, quam esse charum & gratum. Gratiam enim dici, quia per illam homo fit Deo gratus: charitatem vero, quoniam per illam homo redditur Deo charus.
english: Thesis XXIII. Some, on the other hand, such as Durandus, hold that there is no difference at all between grace and charity. They say the two are not distinguished even in concept, only in name.

Charity and grace, on this view, are no more distinct than being dear and being pleasing: it is called grace because by it a man becomes pleasing (gratus) to God, and charity because by it he is made dear (charus) to God.

source_text: XXIV. Sed alii magno numero mediam quodammodo viam insistunt. Dicunt enim gratiam & charitatem neque omnino esse indistinctas, neque tamen reipsa, sed solum ratione distingui. Nimirum haec est eorum sententia, unum atque eundem habitum, qua parte subjectum respicit, atque hominem ipsum in quo inest exornat, Deoque gratum & amabilem reddit, gratiam nominari: qua parte vero respicit opus, & voluntatem promptam efficit ad Deum super omnia diligendum, illum proprie dici charitatem. Quae sententia est Bellarmini lib. 1. de Gratia & Lib. Arbitrio cap. 6.
english: Thesis XXIV. A great many others take a kind of middle way. They say that grace and charity are not wholly indistinct, yet are distinguished not in reality but only in concept.

Their view is that one and the same habit is called grace insofar as it looks to its subject, adorns the man in whom it dwells and makes him pleasing and lovable to God. Insofar as it looks to the work and makes the will ready to love God above all things, it is properly called charity. This is Bellarmine's view (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 6).

source_text: XXV. Quod attinet ad gratiam actualem, sive, ut loquitur Bellarminus, gratiam Auxilii specialis, ut quid eo nomine designent intelligatur, notandum est primo auxilia quibus Deus hominem in agendo adjuvat, in Scholis distingui solere in interna, & externa. Externa sunt occasiones & opportunitates agendi, exempla, consilia, praecepta, hortationes, & plura quae singula persequi longum esset: interna in quibusdam animi motibus consistunt. Auxilia externa non pertinent ad gratiam illam de qua jam quaestio est, sed ad interna restringitur.
english: Thesis XXV. As for actual grace, or the grace of special help as Bellarmine calls it, to see what they mean by the term we must first note that the schools usually divide the helps by which God assists a man in acting into internal and external.

External helps are occasions and opportunities for acting, examples, counsels, precepts, exhortations and many others it would take too long to go through one by one. Internal helps consist in certain motions of the soul. External helps have nothing to do with the grace now in question, which is confined to the internal ones.

source_text: XXVI. Rursus illud Dei auxilium internum, quo homines in agendo egent, Schola Romana distinguit in Generale & in speciale. Auxilium generale vocant, illud quo Deus cum omnibus creaturis concurrit, & in agendo iis cooperatur, sive bene, sive etiam male agant: sive ea quae faciunt sint intra naturae vires atque modum, sive naturam quadantenus superent. Nam juxta communem Scholae Romanae sensum, in ipsis malis actibus quod positivum est bonum est, nec fieri nisi Deo cooperante potest. Auxilium vero speciale dicitur, quod non datur a Deo, nisi ad actus bonos, & qui vires naturae excedunt. Ac proinde gratia auxilii specialis a Bellarmino definitur, Motio Dei qua homo ad operationes, quae naturam suam aliquo modo superant, adjuvatur.
english: Thesis XXVI. The Roman School further divides this internal help of God, which men need in order to act, into general and special. General help is the help by which God concurs with all creatures and works with them in their acting, whether they act well or badly, and whether what they do lies within the powers and scope of nature or goes somewhat beyond it.

For in the common view of the Roman School whatever is positive even in evil acts is good, and cannot come about without God's cooperation. Special help is help that God gives only for good acts that exceed the powers of nature.
So Bellarmine defines the grace of special help as 'the motion of God by which man is helped toward actions that in some way surpass his nature'.

source_text: XXVII. Observat autem ille operationem aliquam tribus modis naturae vires superare posse. Primo simpliciter & absolute. Ut si operatio ex suo genere sit ordinis altioris quam sint res naturales. Quales sunt actus virtutum Theologicarum fidei, spei, & charitatis, quae non acquiruntur per iteratos & frequentatos actus, sed divinitus in animam infunduntur. Secundo non simpliciter, sed ratione status peccati; quoniam homo per peccatum debilitatus multa non potest sine tali auxilio facile efficere. Tertio ratione modi, loci, temporis, aut alterius cujuslibet circumstantiae: quoniam contingere potest, ut id quod neque ex genere suo, neque ratione status, vires naturae superat, easdem tamen superet ratione circumstantiae. Ita, inquit, poterit homo justus praeceptum aliquod Decalogi facile adimplere, si nulla extrinsecus diabolica tentatio accedat. Si vero ejusmodi tentatio accedat, sine speciali auxilio id facere non poterit.
english: Thesis XXVII. Bellarmine observes that an action can surpass the powers of nature in three ways. The first is simply and absolutely, when the action is by its kind of a higher order than natural things. Such are the acts of the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity, which are not acquired by repeated practice but are infused into the soul by God.
The second is not simply but because of the state of sin, since man, weakened by sin, cannot easily do many things without such help.

The third is because of manner, place, time or some other circumstance: something that does not exceed nature's powers by its kind or because of man's state may still exceed them because of the circumstances. 'So,' he says, 'a righteous man will easily be able to keep some commandment of the Decalogue if no temptation from the devil comes upon him from outside. But if such temptation comes, he will not be able to do it without special help.'

source_text: XXVIII. Itaque ad gratiam actualem pertinent, ex doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia, omnes boni & salutares motus, quos in animis nostris Deus excitat. Qui motus & Dei sunt, quoniam ab eo procedunt: & nostri quoque, quoniam sunt actiones vitales, a facultatibus nostris, Deo speciali modo movente, elicitae.
english: Thesis XXVIII. In the view of the doctors of the Roman School, then, actual grace covers all the good and saving motions God stirs up in our souls.
These motions are God's, because they come from him. They are ours too, because they are vital acts drawn out of our own faculties as God moves them in a special way.

source_text: XXIX. Boni autem illi motus, vel intellectum spectant, quales sunt internae illuminationes & cogitationes piae a Deo immissae, ac uno verbo quaelibet illustrationes & inspirationes, quibus mens in veritatis salutiferae notitiam ducitur: vel voluntatem, ut pia desideria & salutares motus atque affectus, quibus immediate voluntas afficitur.
english: Thesis XXIX. These good motions concern either the intellect or the will. Those of the intellect are inward illuminations and devout thoughts sent by God, in a word any enlightenings and inspirations that lead the mind to know saving truth.
Those of the will are devout desires and saving motions and affections that touch the will directly.

source_text: XXX. Rursus autem Gregorius de Valentia, clarioris doctrinae causa, motus qui ad actualem gratiam reducuntur, in duo genera distinguit. Unum, inquit, continetur iis motibus, quibus Deus mentes nostras excitat, vocat, & invitat, ut ad ipsum per fidem, spem, charitatem, poenitentiam, & hujusmodi actiones convertantur. Alterum continetur his motibus, seu actionibus, quibus Deo excitanti, vocanti, & invitanti respondemus, & aperimus mentis nostrae januam, quum ad eum convertimur. Tomo 2. Disput. 8. quaestione 3. puncto 2.
english: Thesis XXX. Gregory of Valencia, to make the teaching clearer, divides the motions that belong to actual grace into two kinds.

'One kind,' he says, 'consists of the motions by which God rouses, calls and invites our minds to turn to him through faith, hope, charity, repentance and acts of that sort. The other consists of the motions or acts by which we answer God as he rouses, calls and invites us, and open the door of our mind when we turn to him' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 2).

source_text: XXXI. Prioris generis motus, juxta ipsum, sunt indeliberati, & physice tantum non libere a facultatibus nostris eliciti: posterioris vero liberi sunt & deliberati. Ad prius genus pertinent piae cogitationes & pia desideria, absque nostro consensu immediate a Deo immissa: ad posterius vero, omnes virtutum Christianarum actus, quos Dei gratia juvante elicimus.
english: Thesis XXXI. According to him, the motions of the first kind are indeliberate: our faculties produce them only physically, not freely. Those of the second kind are free and deliberate.

The first kind covers devout thoughts and devout desires that God sends directly, without our consent. The second covers all the acts of the Christian virtues that we bring forth with the help of God's grace.

source_text: XXXII. Praeterea gratia auxilii specialis, sive, ut aliis dicitur, actualis, dividi solet in gratiam excitantem, & gratiam adjuvantem; seu, ut loquitur Bellarminus, in auxilium excitans, & auxilium adjuvans. Quae distinctio non eodem modo a Theologis Scholae Romanae exponitur. Bellarminus, & omnes cum eo Jesuitae, aliique plurimi, ad gratiam excitantem, quam vocantem etiam appellant, dicunt pertinere divinas illustrationes, & inspirationes, quibus Deus cor nostrum pulsat, ut a somno peccati, vel negligentiae in bonis operibus excitemur. Ad gratiam autem adjuvantem, seu auxilii adjuvantis, spectare divinam cooperationem, directionem, & protectionem, quibus juvamur, tum ut eligamus, tum ut faciamus quod Deus praeveniens inspiravit. Juxta illud Apoc. 3. Ecce sto ad ostium & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam, intrabo ad illum, &c. Quae sunt verba Bellarmini lib. 1. de lib. Arbitrio cap. 2.
english: Thesis XXXII. The grace of special help, or actual grace as others call it, is usually divided into rousing grace and assisting grace, or in Bellarmine's terms into rousing help and assisting help. The theologians of the Roman School do not all explain this distinction the same way.

Bellarmine and all the Jesuits with him, and very many others, say that rousing grace, which they also call calling grace, covers the divine enlightenings and inspirations by which God knocks at our heart to wake us from the sleep of sin or of slackness in good works.

Assisting grace, or the grace of assisting help, they say, covers God's cooperation, guidance and protection, by which we are helped both to choose and to do what God, going before us, has inspired. So Revelation 3: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice, I will come in to him', and so on. These are Bellarmine's words (book 1, On Free Choice, chapter 2).

source_text: XXXIII. Atque eodem recidit expositio Gregorii de Valentia. Nam gratiam vocantem, seu excitantem, inquit, appellant Theologi divinas quasdam inspirationes, seu motus quosdam divinitus in mente hominis excitatos, quibus Deus hominem ad se allicit & invitat, & ad actiones pias atque salutares movet, ut fidei, spei, charitatis, & poenitentiae actibus convertatur. Gratiam autem adjuvantem appellant, Dei dona & beneficia, quibus Deus hominem divinae vocationi & excitationi consentientem adjuvat, tum in eo ipso quod consentit & convertitur, tum in aliis actionibus pietatis, per quas contenditur ad beatitudinem. Itaq; ad hanc gratiam adjuvantem in primis pertinet quod Deus peculiari concursu cum homine cooperatur ad conversionem, id est, ad credendum, sperandum, diligendum, poenitendum, &c. Item quod hominem singulari cura & providentia custodit, & protegit a malo, & dirigit atque stimulat ab bonum, & ei variis inspirationibus, ad vincendas tentationes, & ad observanda mandata robur praebet. Tom. 2. disput. 8. quaest. 3. punct. 3.
english: Thesis XXXIII. Gregory of Valencia's account comes to the same thing. 'Theologians,' he says, 'give the name calling or rousing grace to certain divine inspirations, motions stirred up by God in a man's mind, by which God draws and invites the man to himself and moves him to devout and saving actions, so that he may turn to God by acts of faith, hope, charity and repentance.

They call assisting grace those gifts and benefits by which God helps a man who consents to the divine calling and rousing: both in the very act of consenting and turning, and in the other acts of devotion by which one presses on toward blessedness.

So this assisting grace includes first of all God's special concurrence with man in conversion, that is, in believing, hoping, loving, repenting and so on. It also includes his guarding man with particular care and providence, protecting him from evil, directing and spurring him to good, and giving him strength through various inspirations to overcome temptations and keep the commandments' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 3).
